"If he did not mention." If he did not say an expression of thanksgiving at both the beginning and the end, he is required to repeat. This appears from the Tur. One should say "at every time and at every hour," because "times" include periods of cold and heat, and one who changes the wording is mistaken. [Darchei Moshe; Mateh Moshe] Amen is not answered here, because this is not the end of the blessing. The only reason people commonly pause here is because of Al HaNissim. See siman 284.

"And women," etc. This requires study, because the passage begins with 2 matters and ends with only 1. Tosafos at the beginning of Perek Mi SheMeito explicitly state that women should not say covenant and Torah, and Tosafos and Rashi in Arachin write likewise. Berachos 48b states: covenant does not apply to women; Torah and kingship do not apply to women or servants. This requires study, unlike Olat Tamid and Levush, and it also requires study what basis women now have for reciting these phrases. Lechem Chamudot strained to provide a reason. Bedek HaBayit writes that women are like men because a man is not called a complete person until he has a wife, and the 2 are therefore considered 1 body. This too is a strained defense of the custom.

In my view there is another difficulty. We rule in siman 47 that women recite Birkat HaTorah because they are obligated to learn the mitzvot that apply to them, and the same is ruled in Yoreh De'ah siman 246, seif 6. We also expound, "Thus shall you say to the house of Yaakov," as referring to the women. Why, then, should women not say, "Your Torah that You taught us"? Furthermore, Avodah Zarah 27a states that according to the view derived from "he shall surely perform the milah," a woman is considered within the category of those associated with milah, whereas according to the view derived from "and you shall keep My covenant," women are not members of the covenant. It is therefore possible that women can say, "Your covenant that You sealed in our flesh," because they are treated as belonging to that category.

The statement that Rav Chisda did not say covenant and Torah was in a case in which he led zimun and discharged women. He therefore omitted covenant and Torah because these matters are not equal in women and men. Men actually bear the sign of brit milah and study the entire Torah. This is why he held that if these phrases were omitted, one nevertheless fulfilled the obligation.

The pronunciation of "lo chiser lanu" and "al yechsar lanu" should follow the vocalization recorded by the authorities. "She'atah zan" has a kamatz under the shin. "B'fi kol chai" is read as a construct phrase; see siman 51. Shelah writes to say "chaser yechsar," because the numerical value of the vowels equals that of "lechem."

Seif katan 1, "well," etc. "And now," etc. The view of the Shulchan Aruch is the view of the Rosh, who does not count HaTov VeHaMeitiv itself among the 3 expressions of beneficence. HaTov VeHaMeitiv was instituted concerning those killed at Beitar: "HaTov," because their bodies did not decompose, and "VeHaMeitiv," because permission was given to bury them. Accordingly, 3 additional expressions of beneficence must be said. He therefore separates these 3 and says concerning each one, "He has done good to us," etc. The prevalent custom, by contrast, counts HaTov VeHaMeitiv itself among the 3 expressions, treating "HaTov" and "HaMeitiv" as 2, so that "He did good, does good, and will do good" is counted as the remaining unit. According to this custom, the words "He" and "to us" are said only once so that the phrases are joined together.

"Rather, he should say Kel every day," etc. Taz writes that even the word "Kel" should not be said there, and one should begin "every day," because he already said "the good King," etc.; see there. The exact wording should avoid unnecessary repetition of Divine descriptions and should preserve the sequence established by the earlier authorities.

The blessing HaTov VeHaMeitiv is not one of the original 3 Torah blessings of Birkat HaMazon, but was later instituted at Yavneh concerning the dead of Beitar. This explains several distinctions in its wording and why Amen is answered after Boneh Yerushalayim before beginning it. The expressions "He has done good to us, He does good to us, and He will do good to us" correspond to past, present, and future beneficence. According to the Rosh's formulation they are 3 distinct expressions beyond HaTov VeHaMeitiv itself, while according to the prevalent wording the count is arranged differently.

One should therefore follow the established nusach of his community and not create combinations of the phrases that would duplicate the same expression or disturb the intended count. The purpose of the discussion is to explain the textual variants and the numerical arrangement of the expressions of goodness, not to alter the essential blessing established by the Sages.

He recites Borei Pri HaGafen, etc. See Tosafos in Perek Arvei Pesachim and Rosh for the reason Birkat HaMazon differs from other matters that require a cup. In those other cases Borei Pri HaGafen is recited first, whereas here Borei Pri HaGafen is recited last; see there. We say "Savri Maranan" even though the throat is empty, so that the blessing over wine should not be treated differently from one setting to another. The same applies to Kiddush and Havdalah. Several reasons are given why "Savri" is said over wine but not over beer. I found 1 reason: wine brought a curse upon mankind in the days of Noach, when he became intoxicated and the descendants of Canaan were cursed. We therefore say "Savri," meaning: understand that I intend to drink, and with your consent I drink so that no harm should result. For this reason the listeners customarily answer, "Lechaim."

There, seif 3: A non-Jew is not included in a zimun, and even a convert who underwent brit milah but has not immersed is not included. Note: See Magen Avraham, who writes that this applies whenever he did not immerse properly, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 124, seif 2. In my humble opinion, no proof can be brought from there. There the issue is a stringency concerning wine handled by one whose immersion was defective. Here, however, if the conversion is valid by Torah law and the defect in the immersion is only rabbinic, he is a convert by Torah law and is obligated in Birkat HaMazon, so why should he not join the zimun? He is no worse than the categories that the Sages allowed to join where the basic Jewish status exists.

An example is immersion that was not performed before a beit din of 3. In Yoreh De'ah, siman 268, the Rif and Rambam are cited as regarding this defect as rabbinic in certain circumstances, and the children born afterward retain their status. The Gemara's wording also indicates that the decisive case is one who underwent brit milah but did not immerse at all. Had an improperly constituted immersion been equivalent to no immersion whatsoever, the Gemara could have stated the greater novelty.

The same reasoning applies to the proof from Berachos. Complete absence of immersion prevents completion of conversion, whereas a defect in the manner of immersion that is only rabbinic does not necessarily prevent one from joining a zimun when his Jewish status is valid by Torah law. Therefore Magen Avraham's extension requires study.

A non-Jew is not included in a zimun. Even a convert who underwent brit milah but has not immersed is not included in a zimun. A complete convert, however, is included in a zimun and may recite Birkat HaMazon and say, "for the land that You granted to our fathers."

16) Over arrope one recites SheHakol; this is straightforward. Beit Yosef in the name of Orchot Chaim. Arrope is made by pressing grapes and, after pressing, placing a certain known white earth into the grape juice for 1 hour or longer, so that the wine produced from it clarifies quickly and retains its sweetness. It is then heated until it reaches yad soledet bo temperature. Sherbet is made similarly. My view likewise is that one should recite SheHakol over it, and I believe this is the custom in Constantinople. Knesset HaGedolah, Responsa, volume 2, siman 1; Yad Aharon there, Hagahot Beit Yosef, paragraph 1. Birkei Yosef, paragraph 2, likewise writes in the name of R' Avraham Azulai that over arrope, which is congealed grape juice, one recites SheHakol. The same applies to cooked grapes called trankopit and to kamardin made from apricots; one recites SheHakol. See below, siman 204, paragraph 63. Know that some people of deeds do not eat the kamardin sold in the market, because it is known that market producers prepare large quantities together and may include worm-infested fruit. Flying insects or crawling insects may also develop in it. They eat it only after it has been soaked in water and strained.

"And bread." See Taz. Bach concludes regarding Borei Pri HaGafen that if the taste is that of vinegar but the smell is that of wine and no surface film has formed, or even if a film has formed but the taste remains that of wine, one recites Borei Pri HaGafen. If a film has formed and the taste is that of vinegar, one recites SheHakol. Regarding Kiddush, however, if the taste is that of vinegar, or if the disqualifying film alone has formed, one does not recite Kiddush over it. The fact that Kiddush may be recited over wine containing small white specks after it is strained does not contradict this, because the white film described here is more substantial than those specks; alternatively, the term refers to the beginning of souring. See there.

For practical halacha one should rule like Taz in siman 272, seif katan 3, and Magen Avraham, seif katan 2, agrees. This is why the Mechaber there did not mention the taste explicitly: it is self-evident that one does not recite Borei Pri HaGafen when it has the taste of vinegar, even if the film has not formed. The Rama's statement can be understood as applying even in the morning, and it does not acquire the status of chamar medinah. See there, seif 9. A white film disqualifies wine for Kiddush and is not comparable to the small white specks. See Magen Avraham, siman 272, letter 4, who agrees with Bach on this point. With God's help it will be explained there, and there is no need to elaborate here.

"Divine Name and kingship." The Amidah does not include an explicit formula of kingship in each blessing. Beit Yosef answers in the name of the Rosh that the first blessing, because it contains the words "the great God," is regarded as containing kingship, and all the subsequent blessings follow the first.

Rambam writes in chapter 11 of Hilchot Berachos that one who performs a mitzvah without first reciting its blessing acts as follows. If the mitzvah is an ongoing one, such as tzitzit, tefillin, or sukkah, he recites the blessing afterward while the mitzvah is still being performed. But if he slaughtered, covered the blood, performed a brit milah, or completed another comparable act without a blessing, he does not return and recite the blessing after the act has ended. See Magen Avraham. See also Even HaOzer, who questions the Shulchan Aruch's ruling that if one omitted the word "ha'olam" he must repeat the blessing.

Seif 7, "over," etc. The Yerushalmi cited above asks the relevant questions and, according to one text, says concerning his companions, "he recites a blessing." Beit Yosef explains that the words "he recites a blessing" resolve all the questions: one recites the blessing concerning his father, his teacher, a distinguished person, and a person through whom sanctification occurred, etc. Tur, however, explains that the statement was said only concerning a distinguished person, etc. According to our text of the Yerushalmi, which asks concerning Daniel and his companions and concerning the miracle of the tribes, and does not contain the words "he recites a blessing," none of these questions is resolved. See Magen Avraham. The Yerushalmi should read "if there was a person," and not "and if there was," etc. "Therefore," etc. Gemara, Berachos 57b.

Seif 5, "one purchased," etc. This is as explained above in seif 2 and as stated in the Gemara concerning harvesting, etc. "Which is," etc. This is the view of the Rosh. His words are weak, for if the distinction depends on whether others share the benefit, then the giver should also recite a blessing, apart from the other difficulties. The Yerushalmi, however, holds that the distinction does not depend upon whether there are others who share the benefit. Rather, where a genuinely new benefit comes to a person, such as a found object, a gift, the birth of a male child, an inheritance, and similar events, the blessing is HaTov VeHaMeitiv. When he purchases an item, exchanging money for utensils, the blessing is Shehecheyanu.

This was also the assumption of the questioner in our Gemara from the passage discussing whether there are others who share in the benefit, and from the cases of building a house and the baraita concerning harvesting. This indicates that the rule applies specifically to cases resembling building or acquisition. Rain, by contrast, is always associated with HaTov VeHaMeitiv. See Magen Avraham, who left the matter requiring study. See also the first chapter of Kiddushin, where the case concerns specifically a wealthy and distinguished person, and his difficulty is thereby resolved.

"Some say even a poor person." Specifically a woolen garment and similar items resemble something that comes from time to time, because ordinary people acquire new ones only at intervals. This differs from inexpensive articles that ordinary people commonly replace frequently. "And this is the custom." Radbaz writes that Tosafos were discussing a wealthy person, but a poor person recites the blessing. Conversely, an extremely wealthy person who purchases important utensils but derives no joy from them and does not regard them as significant should not recite the blessing. "From animal hides." The law depends upon the joy and significance of the new article, subject to the distinctions stated by the authorities regarding garments made from animal hides.
